ai.description: The gharial reaches 3.5–6 meters in length and is olive-brown. It is distinguished by an extremely long, thin snout and a bulbous, hollow growth (ghara) at the tip of the male's muzzle.
ai.identificationRemarks: The gharial is uniquely distinguished by its extremely long, narrow, and thin snout, which is lined with numerous interlocking, needle-like teeth for catching fish.
ai.habitat: The gharial inhabits deep, fast-flowing freshwater rivers with sandy banks and sparse riparian vegetation, typically found at low altitudes across the Indian subcontinent.
ai.behavior: Gharials are specialized piscivores that use their long, slender snouts to sweep through water, snapping up fish with rapid, sideways movements of their needle-like teeth.
ai.reproductionNotes: Gharials are oviparous, nesting in sandy riverbanks during the dry season (March–April). Females lay clutches of 30–50 eggs, which hatch after 70–90 days.
ai.distributionRemarks: The gharial is native to the major river systems of northern India and Nepal, primarily inhabiting low-elevation freshwater habitats within the Indo-Gangetic plains.
